pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.05 Introduction to Geopolitics - Answers.pdf
question_en: Regarding geopolitics, which of the following statements is correct?
option_a: Nationalization occurs mainly in nonvital economic sectors.
option_b: Free exchange of currencies can leave countries vulnerable.
option_c: National security tools are used more when state actors cooperate.
explanation_en: Geopolitical tools Tool type Examples Alliances (eg, NATO) National security Armed conflict Espionage Multilateral trade agreements (eg, NAFTA) Economic Nationalization Free exchange of currencies Permitting foreign investments Financial Reducing access to local currency markets Limiting foreign investments Governments can use financial tools to strengthen (or weaken) their relationships with other countries. Cooperative financial tools include: allowing more free exchange of international currencies, and encouraging foreign investments. Noncooperative financial tools include: restricting access to local currency markets, and discouraging foreign investments. Although the free exchange of currencies can benefit participant countries, it can also create vulnerabilities in the international financial system. For instance, many countries openly borrow from and lend to each other in US dollars. This exposes participants to risk of a change in US monetary policy that may impact the real value of the US dollar. (Choice A) Nationalization is an economic tool that involves a government seizing control of a private sector. It is most common in sectors perceived vital to economic security or competitiveness. (Choice C) Governments typically cooperate with each other (eg, in treaty organizations such as NATO) to minimize the need to use national security tools (eg, armed conflict).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.05 Introduction to Geopolitics - Answers.pdf
question_en: For an investor with a long-term investment horizon, the most appropriate response to a new, high-velocity geopolitical risk is to adjust a portfolio's:
explanation_en: Framework for assessing geopolitical risks Likelihood Probability that a geopolitical risk will occur Velocity How quickly the risk will impact investment returns Impact Size of impact and breadth of impact Analysts evaluate geopolitical risks by assessing the: likelihood that they will occur, velocity of impact, and size and nature of impact. Velocity describes the speed of impact on investment returns. High-velocity risks have short-term impacts and create short-term market volatility (eg, 1987 stock market crash). Investors may capitalize on such market dislocations via tactical asset allocations (ie, short-term shifts in asset class composition of a portfolio). (Choice A) Investors typically shift sector allocations in response to medium-velocity risks, which have medium-term impacts and may negatively impact a company's operations and reduce cash flows, thereby reducing valuation (eg, a crop disease decimates potato harvests for more than one season). (Choice C) Changes to strategic asset allocation may be warranted by low-velocity risks that have major long-term impacts due to changes to asset class returns and risks.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.06 International Trade - Answers.pdf
question_en: Trading bloc members would most likely use a common currency in a:
explanation_en: Trading blocs are formal agreements that reduce or eliminate barriers to trade. An economic union is a type of trading bloc characterized by the greatest amount of economic integration and cooperation among its members. In addition to features of a common market, economic unions share common economic institutions (eg, one central bank for all members) and policies. Economic unions may also elect to adopt a common currency (eg, members of the European Union use the euro as their currency). An economic union that adopts a common currency is known as a monetary union. (Choice A) A free trade area is a common trading bloc that eliminates barriers such as tariffs on goods and services between members. However, it lacks both coordinated trade policies against nonmembers and free movement of labor and capital between members. (Choice C) A common market shares many characteristics of an economic union, but it does not have common economic institutions or policies. Nor does it adopt a common currency.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.06 International Trade - Answers.pdf
question_en: Several countries have signed an agreement creating a trading bloc. The agreement allows tariff-free trade in goods and services among members and requires that they impose the same tariffs on imports from all nonmembers. However, the movement of people and capital among members is restricted. This trading bloc is best described as a:
explanation_en: Trading blocs are groups of countries that have signed agreements designed to increase trade. The agreements can narrowly focus on trade in goods and services or encompass additional considerations such as movement of the factors of production (ie, capital and labor) or common external trade policies. Customs unions allow tariff-free trade in goods and services among members and require that member countries have common trade policies (eg, tariffs) with all nonmember countries. However, customs unions do not allow free movement of people or capital among member countries. (Choice B) Free trade areas (FTAs) allow tariff-free trade in goods and services among member countries. However, FTAs neither require common trade policies with nonmember countries nor allow free movement of people or capital among member countries. (Choice C) Common markets allow tariff-free trade in goods and services and free movement of people and capital among member countries. Members also have common trade policies with all nonmember countries.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.06 International Trade - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following trade policies is most appropriate for a country to enact if it is trying to reduce a large trade deficit?
option_a: Reduce import tariffs on raw materials and manufactured goods by an average of 50%.
option_b: Impose import quotas limiting foreigners to 20% of a domestic market in which imports constitute 5% of the market.
option_c: Negotiate a voluntary export restraint agreement with a country running a large trade surplus
explanation_en: Quotas, tariffs, and voluntary export restraints are the policies most commonly used to reduce trade deficits. Imposing quotas or levying tariffs on imports directly impacts commercial counterparties. Alternatively, agreements with foreign governments are used to restrain their firms from exporting to the domestic market. Although the specific mechanisms of each policy differ, all restrict foreign sales in the domestic market. All else constant, the trade balance is favorably affected as reduced imports shrink trade deficits or increase trade surpluses. Voluntary export restraints are negotiated with countries currently running large surpluses. Foreign governments agreeing to constrain their exports will reduce domestic imports. Effective voluntary export restraint agreements reduce trade deficits. (Choice A) Reducing tariffs on raw materials and manufactured goods tends to make those foreign-sourced items less expensive. Tariff cuts increase imports, which leads to higher trade deficits. (Choice B) Import quotas normally reduce trade deficits. Limiting foreign producers to a 20% market share in a market where foreign sales account for only 5% of sales is an ineffective way to reduce the trade deficit.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.06 International Trade - Answers.pdf
question_en: Unlike members of a customs union, members of a common market most likely:
option_b: maintain uniform trade policies with nonmembers.
option_c: may freely move factors of production between members.
explanation_en: Trading blocs are formal agreements that reduce or eliminate barriers to trade. They can be bilateral or multilateral and are classified based on the topics covered by the agreement. Common markets and customs unions are both characterized by an absence of tariffs for goods and services between members, as well as common trade policies imposed against all nonmembers (Choice B). However, a common market is broader than a customs union in that it also allows members to move labor and capital (ie, factors of production) among other members. This means that a manufacturer headquartered in Country A can build a factory in Country B and staff it with citizens of Country A and other member countries. This would not be allowed if the countries' trading bloc were only a customs union. (Choice A) A common currency can be adopted by members of an economic union. An economic union is considered the broadest type of trading bloc. It incorporates all the characteristics of a common market shown above in addition to having common economic institutions (eg, one central bank for all members) and policies.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.06 International Trade - Answers.pdf
question_en: An analyst has compiled the following information: Country Z is an open economy, trading at world prices, and does not currently trade with any of the other three countries. Assuming equal consumption of both commodities, which country will benefit the most from a trading relationship with Country Z?
explanation_en: An autarky is a country that produces all goods and services consumed internally and does not trade with others. An autarkic economy is considered a closed economy. Domestic prices within a country are a function of its ability to produce those goods with only domestic resources and are known as the autarkic prices. Countries that do not place restrictions on imports and exports are known as open economies. Open economies are said to practice free trade as they import and export at the world's price for goods and services (eg, Country Z). The further away the world price is relative to a country's autarkic price, the greater the potential trade benefit for the autarky. A country's terms of trade benefit the most if world export prices are greater than its autarkic price and world import prices are less than its autarkic price since the country can achieve greater purchasing power. In this scenario, all the autarkies produce coffee below world price and sugar above world price. Thus, if all three traded with other countries, each would export coffee and import sugar. The net terms-of-trade improvement would be greatest for Country A since it would sell (ie, export) coffee at the world price of $1.10 and buy (ie, import) sugar at the world price of $0.40, netting a $0.50 improvement. (Choices B and C) The net terms-of-trade improvement for Country B is $0.15. For Country C, it is $0.40.

question_en: A country recently imposed a tariff on apples of €300 per metric ton. The pre-tariff price for apples was €2,000 per metric ton. The table below shows the quantity demanded and the quantity supplied by domestic producers, along with the pre- and post-tariff prices of apples: The image below shows the market for apples in this country: The area labeled A in the image represents an increase in:
explanation_en: A tariff is one type of trade restraint. It is a tax on imported goods that is usually paid as a higher price for the goods and usually results in a loss to the net welfare of the economy. Tariffs cause inefficiencies in both the supply and production functions of the economy; these losses are known as deadweight losses. In the diagram above, the supply deadweight loss is Region B and the demand deadweight loss is Region D. Before the tariff, all suppliers had per-unit production costs of €200 or less. The tariff caused the price to increase to €250 so domestic suppliers whose production costs were greater than €200 could now compete. However, domestic supply increased (from 4 million to 6.5 million) while domestic demand decreased (from 8.2 million to 7 million), therefore the additional domestic supply represented a reallocation of resources to phones when those resources could have been better employed elsewhere in the economy, creating an inefficiency. The demand deadweight loss is evidenced from the reduced domestic demand after the tariff. Consumers who might have spent more than €200 for a phone but would not spend €250 were excluded from the market. The deadweight loss is the sum of the areas of the triangles B and D: Compare types of trade restrictions, such as tariffs, quotas, and export subsidies, and their economic implications

question_en: A country that is a price taker in the international market imposes a per-unit tariff of €50 on imported mobile phones. The table below shows domestic consumption, domestic production, and mobile phone prices before and after the tariff's imposition: The total deadweight loss (in €) from the imposition of the tariff is closest to:
explanation_en: Most economists believe greater overall welfare is attained when countries engage in international trade rather than by attempting self-sufficiency in meeting domestic demand (ie, autarky). The gains from international trade derive from each country concentrating on the production of goods it produces relatively more efficiently and trading for goods it produces relatively less efficiently. Gains result from specialization and economies of scale. The gains from trade are not shared equally; there are winners and losers. On one hand, industries expanding to meet export opportunities will benefit from higher prices, due to increased foreign demand, and their employees will benefit from greater job opportunities and higher wages (Choice C). On the other hand, the industries' domestic customers must pay higher prices. In addition, industries facing import competition will suffer domestic market share decline. As such industries contract, they will employ fewer workers. (Choice A) Increased trade results in greater consumer choice. This is due both to imported goods competing with domestic suppliers and the introduction of previously unavailable products.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.06 International Trade - Answers.pdf
question_en: A country initiating a free trade agreement with its major trading partners is least likely to experience:
option_a: a wider variety of goods available to consumers.
option_b: increased employment in industries facing import competition.
option_c: higher wages in industries that expand due to increased exports.
explanation_en: A voluntary export restraint (VER) is a method that governments use to reduce trade deficits and protect domestic producers. With a VER, an exporting country's government agrees to limit exports of a certain good or set of goods to an importing country, typically at the request of the importing country's government. The exporting country may agree to a VER to avoid a stricter tariff or import quota. For the importing (ie, domestic) country, a VER operates in the same way as an import quota to limit imports. However, since the limit is imposed by the exporting (ie, foreign) government, the domestic government does not receive any quota rent. Therefore, a VER allows a domestic government to limit the volume of imports of a good, but it does not increase the domestic government's revenues. (Choice A) A tariff aims to limit imports of specific goods into a domestic country by setting a tax on the imported goods. This raises the cost for foreign producers and increases the price of the goods for domestic producers and consumers. With a tariff, the domestic government generates revenue through the tax collected on the imports. (Choice B) A quota limits the quantity of a good imported into a domestic country. A domestic government can generate revenue under a quota by selling import licenses to foreign exporters. Without licenses, quota rents will likely be captured by foreign exporters.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.07 Capital Flows and the FX Market - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 2.07 Capital Flows and the FX Market
question_en: All else being equal, if the domestic price level decreases relative to the foreign price level, the real exchange rate between the two currencies, when quoted as domestic currency per unit of foreign currency, will most likely:
explanation_en: Real exchange rates measure the relative purchasing power for the goods and services of two currencies and are typically created for economic analysis. Nominal (ie, observed or spot) exchange rates show the price of one currency in terms of another currency and are the quotes used in currency markets for currency purchases and sales. The real exchange rate is calculated by adjusting the nominal exchange rate by the ratio of price levels (ie, relative rate of inflation) in the corresponding countries. By removing the effects of inflation, real exchange rates better represent economic changes to exchange rates over time. The formula shows that the direction of change in real exchange rates (when quoted as domestic currency per unit of foreign currency) is: Directly related to the direction of change in the nominal exchange rate and the direction of change in the foreign price level Inversely related to the direction of change in the domestic price level As a result, if the domestic price level decreases, all else being equal, the real exchange rate will increase (Choices A and B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.07 Capital Flows and the FX Market - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 2.07 Capital Flows and the FX Market
question_en: The exchange rate between the euro (EUR) and the Japanese yen (JPY) is quoted by the amount of JPY per EUR 1 (JPY/EUR). If JPY appreciates against EUR, the spot exchange rate quote will be for a(n):
explanation_en: Currency values are expressed as a ratio of exchange between currencies. In the question, Japanese yen (JPY) is the price currency and the euro (EUR) is the base currency. JPY appreciation against EUR means JPY 1 is worth a greater amount of EUR in Year 1 than it was in Year 0. Since the exchange rate quote is given as the number of JPY per EUR 1, the question requires the relationship between the currencies to be viewed from the opposite perspective, with EUR as the price currency and JPY as the base currency. Appreciation of JPY means the same thing as depreciation of EUR. The EUR depreciation means EUR 1 buys fewer JPY. Consequently, JPY/EUR will be quoted at a lower number since it will take a smaller amount of JPY to buy EUR 1.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.07 Capital Flows and the FX Market - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 2.07 Capital Flows and the FX Market
question_en: An investor wants to diversify into foreign currency-denominated securities while minimizing exchange rate risk. Which of the following currency regimes would expose the investor to the least exchange rate risk?
explanation_en: An investor looking to add foreign currency-denominated investments to a portfolio is exposed not only to asset price risk but also to exchange rate risk. The more potential fluctuation in the exchange rate, the higher the exchange rate risk. A currency regime broadly describes the policies of a country's monetary authority for managing domestic currency exchange rates. Between the extremes of dollarization and independent floating regimes, exchange rate risk increases as regimes allow greater exchange rate flexibility and support increased monetary policy independence. Of the regimes in this scenario, the order from lowest to highest exchange rate risk is: Currency board, a legislative commitment to exchange the domestic currency for a specific foreign currency while holding full reserves against the foreign currency. Minor fluctuations in exchange rates may occur. Hong Kong SAR operates under this regime with the US dollar as the anchor currency. Target zone, a commitment to maintain the exchange rate within a preset range. Syria operates under such a regime (Choice A). Managed float is similar to an independent float since exchange rates are market-determined. However, the monetary authority is more likely to intervene to manage domestic economic measures (eg, the balance of payments). Russia operates under this type of regime (Choice B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.07 Capital Flows and the FX Market - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 2.07 Capital Flows and the FX Market
question_en: A country with a well-respected monetary authority maintains the domestic currency exchange rate within 1% of the US dollar through direct and indirect intervention in the currency markets. The country is most likely using which of the following currency regimes?
explanation_en: A currency regime broadly describes the policies of a country's monetary authority for managing domestic currency exchange rates. A country with its own currency may choose either a fixed-type or floating-type regime. The various regimes reflect a spectrum of exchange rate flexibility and monetary policy independence. A fixed parity regime, often called a fixed peg regime, refers to a country maintaining the domestic currency exchange rate with a specific foreign currency or a basket of foreign currencies (typically from major trading partners) within a narrow range or "band" (typically +/− 1.0%). The monetary authority keeps the exchange rate within this band by selling or buying the foreign currency. A fixed parity regime is often used to increase exchange rate predictability since the foreign currency selected for the peg is typically a more stable or more widely used currency than the domestic currency. The increased exchange rate stability facilitates trading and investment between the country and major foreign partners. (Choice B) Dollarization (a term that does not apply exclusively to the dollar) occurs when countries without their own currency adopt and use a foreign currency for all transactions. (Choice C) A currency board regime differs from a fixed parity regime in that the exchange rate is a legislative commitment to a set rate, and the amount of foreign currency reserves held is nondiscretionary.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.07 Capital Flows and the FX Market - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 2.07 Capital Flows and the FX Market
question_en: A Canadian tourist in Hong Kong needs to exchange Canadian dollars (CAD) for Hong Kong dollars (HKD). A dealer provides a quote of 0.1799 CAD/HKD. Since the inverse of 0.1799 is 5.5586, from the perspective of the Canadian tourist, the dealer's quote is most appropriately described as a(n):
option_a: direct quote of 0.1799 CAD per HKD.
option_b: direct quote of 5.5586 HKD per CAD.
option_c: indirect quote of 0.1799 CAD per HKD.
explanation_en: Exchange rates show the price of one currency per unit of another currency. The two methods of quoting exchange rates are: Direct quotes, domestic currency per unit of foreign currency Indirect quotes, foreign currency per unit of domestic currency Thinking of currency as a consumer good can be helpful. For example, the quote of 0.1799 CAD/HKD means that the Canadian must pay CAD 0.1799 for HKD 1.000 (the good). From the Canadian perspective, this is a direct quote because the Canadian's domestic currency is in the numerator. (Choice B) From the Canadian's perspective, the quote of 5.5586 HKD per CAD is an indirect quote because the foreign currency is in the numerator. Note that this quote is the inverse of the direct quote 0.1799 CAD per HKD. (Choice C) Since indirect quotes have the domestic currency in the denominator, a quote of 0.1799 CAD per HKD is an indirect quote from a Hong Kong resident's, not a Canadian's, perspective.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.07 Capital Flows and the FX Market - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 2.07 Capital Flows and the FX Market
question_en: For this question, assume that GBP is the domestic currency and INR is the foreign currency. If the consumer price index (CPI) in the United Kingdom rises more than the CPI in India, the real INR/GBP exchange rate most likely:
option_a: will decrease, and the purchasing power of the INR will increase.
option_b: will increase, and the purchasing power of the INR will decrease.
option_c: will decrease, and the purchasing power of the INR will decrease.
explanation_en: Purchasing power refers to the amount of goods or services a currency can purchase. Changes in purchasing power are inversely related to changes in relative price levels, which are commonly measured by the consumer price index (CPI). As a country's price level (CPI) rises, its currency's purchasing power falls. Real exchange rates measure the purchasing power of one currency relative to another. All else equal, the real exchange rate moves as a function of changes in the ratio of the foreign CPI to the domestic CPI (assuming no movements in the nominal exchange rate). This is demonstrated with a simple example: If the nominal INR/GBP exchange rate = 10, and the Indian CPI rises by 2% while simultaneously the UK CPI rises by 5%, the expected real exchange rate will be 10 × (1.02 / 1.05) ≈ 9.7142. This means that fewer INR (9.7142 vs. 10) are needed to purchase GBP 1 worth of goods and services: GBP purchasing power has decreased, and INR purchasing power has increased. The smaller increase in the Indian price level (relative to the UK increase) leads to a decrease in the INR/GBP real exchange rate, and thus an increase in the INR purchasing power relative to the GBP purchasing power (Choices B and C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.07 Capital Flows and the FX Market - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 2.07 Capital Flows and the FX Market
question_en: When a country uses dollarization as a currency regime, which of the following is the most likely consequence?
option_a: It loses the ability to set its own monetary policy.
option_b: It maintains foreign currency reserves against its monetary base.
option_c: Domestic bank interest rates are close to those of the adopted country.
explanation_en: A currency regime broadly describes the policies of a country's central bank for managing its currency's exchange rates. Some countries do not have their own currency. Dollarization refers to those countries adopting and using another country's currency for all its transactions. The term "dollarization" derives from the US dollar being the most often adopted currency, but the term does not apply exclusively to the dollar. The main advantage of dollarization as a formal policy is that it imposes fiscal discipline on the adopting country. A country could theoretically print limitless amounts of its own currency to pay its own government debt, but it cannot print the currency of another country. This prevents a country from taking on unsustainable debt loads. However, the trade-off is that the country can no longer set its own monetary policy since it cannot regulate its own money supply. Although a country may adopt the US dollar, there are no protections, such as FDIC deposit insurance, afforded to that country. This lack of protection makes dollarized accounts riskier than accounts in the US, so interest rates for bank accounts in dollarized countries are higher than similar accounts in the US (Choice C). (Choice B) This is characteristic of a currency board system, where a country has its own currency but collateralizes it with foreign currency reserves. There is usually a fixed exchange rate between the domestic and foreign currencies.

A Singapore-based investor holds assets in New Zealand denominated in NZD. The investor forecasts the following changes over the next year:

This formula estimates the net change in the real exchange rate as the expected change in the spot rate, adjusted for the difference between the expected change in the price currency's inflation and the expected change in the base currency's inflation; the three expected changes are expressed as percentage changes. %ΔR ≈ %ΔS + %ΔP − %ΔP = +6% + (−2%) − (+3%) = 1% SGD/NZD SGD/NZD NZD SGD (Choice B) 5% results from incorrectly treating NZD deflation as reinforcing, not offsetting, the impact of the increase in the SGD/NZD spot exchange rate. (Choice C) 11% results from incorrectly treating both NZD deflation and SGD inflation as factors that reinforce the impact of the increase in the SGD/NZD spot exchange rate.

question_en: According to the Marshall-Lerner condition, domestic currency devaluation is least likely to improve a country's trade balance if the mix of imports and exports primarily consists of:
option_c: goods that represent a large portion of a consumer's budget.
explanation_en: Goods with higher price elasticities Have many available substitutes Trade in competitive markets Are considered luxury or discretionary goods Represent a significant portion of consumer spending Represent a significant portion of input costs Exchange rate movements affect a country's trade balance by influencing imports and exports. Devaluation of the domestic currency reduces the cost of a country's exports to foreign buyers and increases the cost of imports to domestic consumers. Therefore, in theory, the quantity of exports demanded will increase and the quantity of imports demanded will decline. However, currency devaluation is just one factor influencing the change in quantity demanded. The Marshall-Lerner condition, part of the elasticity approach to understanding trade balances, asserts that total expenditures on imports and exports are driven by the price elasticities of the traded goods. Under this approach, a devaluation of the domestic currency will be more successful at reducing a trade deficit if the price elasticity of those goods is high. When a product has few substitutes (eg, petroleum, medications), demand may not change in proportion to a change in price. A lack of alternative goods that can satisfy the same desire or purpose results in price inelasticity. A country that exports or imports goods with inelastic demand will probably not improve its trade balance through currency devaluation since total expenditures are unlikely to be affected. (Choices A and C) In general, luxury goods and goods that represent a large portion of consumer budgets have higher price elasticities. Consumers are likely to purchase fewer of these goods when prices increase and more of them when prices decrease.
